summary: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), defined in RFC 8949, is a compact and extensible data format. This document defines CBOR tags for object identifiers (OIDs) and is the reference for the IANA registration of those tags.

eli5.summary: Object identifiers are long numbered names. This document gives them a compact label in a small data format so they take less space.

questions: how to encode an oid in cbor
subtitle: Three CBOR tags that mark a byte string as an ASN.1 object identifier, absolute or relative.

tldr.problem: Many IETF protocols carry object identifiers (OIDs), but CBOR had no standard way to mark a byte string as one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines tags 111 (absolute OID), 110 (relative OID) and 112 (relative to 1.3.6.1.4.1), each wrapping the BER-encoded value bytes of an OID. The tags can also be put on arrays and maps to tag every element at once.
tldr.outcome: CBOR data can now carry OIDs compactly and compatibly with ASN.1 BER. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is the reference for the IANA registrations of the tags and of three CDDL control operators.

today: RFC 9090 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It remains the reference for tags 111, 110 and 112 and for the three CDDL control operators.

sections.title: Why CBOR Needs OID Tags
sections.content:
The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), defined in RFC 8949, carries structured data without a pre-agreed schema. It has a tagging mechanism that extends its set of data types through an IANA registry.

This RFC uses that mechanism for object identifiers (OIDs), which many IETF protocols carry. ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER) already define binary encodings for absolute and relative OIDs. The value part of those encodings fits in a CBOR byte string, so the RFC defines two tags for the two kinds of OID and a third for a common optimization.
sections.eli5: CBOR is a small box for data. Some data are long number-names, and this document adds a sticker that says 'this is a number-name' so everyone reads it the same way.

sections.title: The Three OID Tags
sections.content:
An OID is a sequence of unsigned integers, each one an arc of the international OID tree. BER writes them by concatenating a self-delimiting form of each integer. For an absolute OID, BER also merges the first two integers X and Y into one value, X * 40 + Y, and a decoder reverses that step.

The RFC defines three tags, collectively the OID tags:

  • 111: a byte string holding the BER encoding of an absolute OID.
  • 110: a byte string holding the BER encoding of a relative OID. Since each number is encoded like a Self-Delimiting Numeric Value (SDNV), it can also tag a sequence of zero or more SDNVs.
  • 112: structurally like 110, but understood as relative to 1.3.6.1.4.1, the IANA Private Enterprise Number arc. The result has the semantics of an absolute OID.

Tag 112 exists because companies often use self-assigned numbers under 1.3.6.1.4.1, and that prefix adds 5 fixed bytes to an encoded OID.
sections.eli5: There are three stickers. One is for full addresses, one is for 'start from where we already are', and one is for 'start from the usual company street' so you do not have to write that part every time.

sections.title: Validity of the Tagged Byte String
sections.content:
A byte string tagged with 111, 110 or 112 MUST be syntactically valid BER contents: a concatenation of SDNV values. Each SDNV is one or more bytes whose top bit is set, except the last byte, whose top bit is clear. Two rules follow:

  • The first byte of the string, and any byte after a byte with the top bit clear, MUST NOT be 0x80, so integers have no leading zeroes.
  • The last byte MUST NOT have the top bit set, so there is no incomplete final integer.

If either condition is broken, the tag is invalid. ASN.1 requires a relative OID to have at least one arc, but this specification permits empty relative OIDs; applications may still exclude them. To ease searching for specific OID values, definite length encoding is RECOMMENDED for the byte strings. The RFC also gives byte-level regular expressions for valid contents of tag 111 and of tags 110 and 112.
sections.eli5: Each number must be written the proper way and must not be cut off halfway. If a number is written sloppily or left unfinished, the sticker does not count.

sections.title: Examples and Preferred Serialization
sections.content:
The SHA-256 OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1 has 9 content bytes in BER. In CBOR it becomes D8 6F (tag 111), then 49 (a byte string of 9 bytes), then those 9 bytes. A MIB relative OID .1.1.29 becomes D8 6E, 43 and the 3 bytes 01 01 1D. The RFC notes this saves seven bytes compared to the full OID encoding.

For an absolute OID beginning with 1.3.6.1.4.1, both tag 111 and tag 112 are applicable. The tag 112 form is five bytes shorter, because it leaves out the prefix h'2b06010401'. That shorter form is the preferred serialization, so the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of RFC 8949 require 112 wherever it is possible.
sections.eli5: If a long address starts with the same well-known part, you can skip that part and say 'the usual start'. The shorter way is the one you are supposed to use.

sections.title: Tag Factoring with Arrays and Maps
sections.content:
The content of an OID tag can also be an array or a map. The tag is then factored out of each item and placed on the container.

  • For an array, the tag is imputed to every element that is a byte string, array or map. Other elements, such as text strings or tags, are unaffected.
  • For a map, a tag with the same number is imputed to every key that is a byte string, array or map. Values are not affected.

Nesting works, so one 111 tag around an array of arrays of arrays of byte strings makes a 3-dimensional array of OIDs. The RFC's worked example is an X.500 distinguished name, with attribute-type OIDs as map keys and text values, all under one 111 tag. Its CBOR encoding takes 109 bytes.

When tag factoring is used with 111, some OIDs inside may be shortened with tag 112 instead. The RFC does not make the presence or absence of factoring a preferred serialization; application protocols decide, and must say so if they need deterministic encoding.
sections.eli5: Instead of sticking a label on every jar in a box, you put one label on the box that says 'everything in here is this kind of thing'.

sections.title: CDDL Support
sections.content:
The Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL, RFC 8610) describes CBOR structures. This RFC adds three control operators that apply to byte strings:

  • .sdnv: the byte string is one SDNV matching a control type of unsigned integers.
  • .sdnvseq: the byte string is a sequence of SDNVs that decodes to an array of unsigned integers matching the control type.
  • .oid: like .sdnvseq, but it includes the X*40+Y translation for absolute OIDs.

For example, bytes .oid [2, 5, 4, *uint] matches all OIDs inside the arc 2.5.4. The RFC also recommends CDDL type names: oid = #6.111(bstr), roid = #6.110(bstr) and pen = #6.112(bstr).
sections.eli5: There is also a way to write down the rules for what a message may contain. This document adds a few new words to that rule language for talking about these number-names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8949 apply. The BER encodings are compact and unambiguous but MUST be followed precisely. If the requirements on the byte string are not followed, an attacker may submit alternative representations that a checking process and a later decoder read differently.

OIDs can always be treated as opaque byte strings. Apart from checking the structure requirements, it is strongly NOT RECOMMENDED to process them further, for example by converting to dotted notation and back, unless absolutely necessary. Integer values in OIDs are unlimited in range.

Tag factoring brings its own risk: an attacker might trick an application into using a byte string inside a factored item that was not meant to fall under the tag. Applications therefore need to be restrictive about which data items they apply tag factoring to.
sections.eli5: Be strict about checking that each number-name is written correctly, because a trickster could write one two ways and fool a guard. Do not put one big label on a box unless you are sure everything inside should have it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has assigned tags 111, 110 and 112 in the 1+1 byte space (24..255) of the CBOR Tags registry, with this document as the reference. Each accepts a byte string, array or map as its data item. IANA also registered the CDDL control operators .sdnv, .sdnvseq and .oid in the CDDL Control Operators registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of sticker numbers now has these three entries, and the rule language's word list has three new words.

items.label: Object identifier
items.desc: Byte string with the BER encoding of an absolute OID.

items.label: Relative OID
items.desc: Byte string with the BER encoding of a relative OID, or a sequence of SDNVs.

items.label: Relative to 1.3.6.1.4.1
items.desc: Like 110, but the result is an absolute OID under the Private Enterprise Number arc.
